Reuters:

China has eased limits on refined fuel exports for a second month in August, giving refiners temporary approval to ship 2.7 million metric tons to destinations excluding Hong Kong and Macau, five industry sources with knowledge of the matter said.

Refiners are also allowed to roll over some of the August allowances to September because of the tight timeline for spot sales, two of the people said.

Including shipments to Hong Kong and jet fuel refuelling for international flights at Chinese airports, the August programme is estimated to reach 3.6 million tons for August.

That's an increase from July's total export plans - including shipments to Hong Kong and bonded jet fuel sales - of up to 2.5 million tons, according to estimates.

The quotas cover gasoline, diesel and jet fuel.

The National Development & Reform Commission, which oversees the fuel quotas, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

China began curbing fuel exports in March, with significant cuts through June, to safeguard domestic fuel supply amid disruptions from the Iran war.

The main reason for the delay in reaching an agreement with Oman regarding the Strait of Hormuz is the involvement of the United States and the threats from Trump.

Strait of Hormuz over the last 24 hours: Iranian control

News galore: another MOU is imminent! 

Fog of war? More like fog of news. The inconsistent news flow continues. 

The latest info is that Iran will determine inbound vessel flows AND have a say on what vessels can or cannot exit. Iran is insisting on charging a toll, while the US is saying no.

Earlier in the day, Bessent appeared on TV saying a deal would be announced today, which sent crude down by $3.5/bbl. Late tonight, Axios reported that an announcement will be made tomorrow to reopen the Strait, sending crude down another $1/bbl.

Whatever the case, the market is now fully expecting this deal to be announced. But unlike the June MOU where ~100 million stranded barrels exited, floating storage in the Persian Gulf is only ~23 million bbls this time around. The impact on the physical market will be negligible. 

But now that they've made a big deal about how it will be under Iranian control. Let's see. Let's see what the implementation will be. Will Iran still throttle inflows because of other geopolitical issues? What about the Houthis?

This is far from over. 

Turning over to the video from @MarineTraffic, you can see that the US ran another convoy through the Oman lane. Panama Prosperity and Al Rawdah went through. 

Let's see what happens tomorrow.

Unlike the June MOU where 100+ million bbls of floating storage exited in a hurry, we have ~23 million bbls of floating storage in the Persian Gulf this time around.

The physical oil market will absorb that in a hurry.
